lesson.title: Two Channels, One Transfer: How FTP Separates Commands from Data
lesson.summary: FTP moves files between systems using two separate TCP connections at once, a control connection for commands and replies and a data connection for the actual file bytes, an approach unlike the single connection design of protocols like HTTP or SMTP.
lesson.body:
FTP, the File Transfer Protocol, is one of the oldest application layer protocols still in use, standardized in an RFC and built on top of TCP for the same reason SMTP is: moving a file reliably means every byte has to arrive, in order, without corruption. What sets FTP apart structurally from most of the other protocols covered so far is that it does not send everything over one connection. It deliberately splits communication into two separate TCP connections that exist at the same time: a control connection, conventionally on port 21, which stays open for the duration of a session carrying commands like logging in, listing a directory, or requesting a file, and a separate data connection, opened and closed as needed, which carries nothing but the actual bytes of a file being transferred.

This separation exists so that the control channel stays free to send commands and receive status replies even while a large file transfer is in progress on the data channel, and so that a single control session can be reused for many separate file transfers without renegotiating a login each time. There are two ways the data connection can be opened, and the difference between them matters in practice. In active mode, the client tells the server, over the control connection, which port on the client's own machine to connect back to, and the server initiates a new connection to the client for the data transfer; this requires the server to make an inbound connection to the client, which firewalls and NAT devices on the client's side often block, since they are typically configured to allow outbound connections but not unsolicited inbound ones. In passive mode, the client initiates both connections: it asks the server to open a data port and wait, the server replies with an IP address and port to connect to, and the client connects to it just as it did for the control connection, which is far friendlier to firewalls and NAT and is the more commonly used mode today.

A concrete download illustrates the flow. The client opens the control connection to port 21 and authenticates with USER and PASS commands. It then sends a PASV command asking the server to open a passive data port; the server replies with an IP address and port number for that data connection. The client opens a second TCP connection to that address and port. Only then does the client send RETR followed by a filename over the control connection, and the requested file's bytes stream across the data connection while the control connection sits idle, ready for the next command. Once the transfer finishes, the data connection closes and the server sends a 226 Transfer complete reply back on the control connection, and the client can issue another command, like requesting a different file, without having to log in again.
